vignette:
He is a 54-year-old Middle Eastern man who has spent most of his adult life building a sense of order through logic, routines, and work. He lives alone, has never married, and is known among colleagues as quiet, precise, and reliable. For years he has been the kind of software engineer who can disappear into a problem for hours, finding comfort in code because it behaves predictably. That confidence begins to unravel after a sexual assault that leaves him feeling stripped of the very control he has relied on for decades.

The assault happens later in life than he ever imagined such a thing could happen to him, which makes it harder for him to explain even to himself. In the aftermath, he does not respond with panic right away; instead, he goes numb. He showers repeatedly, as if he can scrub away not only what happened but the fact that it happened to him. He changes clothes, washes them, throws some away, and still feels contaminated. At first he tells himself that if he keeps moving, keeps working, keeps his face neutral, he can contain it. He returns to his job and sits in front of his monitors for long stretches, staring at lines of code without absorbing them. The work that once gave him relief now feels like a task performed underwater.

Over the weeks that follow, he begins to organize his life around avoiding reminders. He takes different routes to the office. He stops going to the gym at certain hours because the locker room feels unsafe. He checks locks multiple times before bed and keeps lights on longer than he used to, though he still sleeps poorly. He falls asleep exhausted, then wakes suddenly with his heart racing, certain for a moment that someone is in the apartment. Some nights the memories come back in fragments—an image, a sensation, a smell—so vivid that he sits up gasping and has to remind himself where he is. He does not describe these moments easily, but his body does: tense shoulders, clenched jaw, restless hands, a constant readiness to startle.

He has always been private, and now privacy turns into isolation. He tells no family members and only one trusted friend knows that something happened, though even that conversation is brief and unfinished. He says he is “fine,” then withdraws. Phone calls go unanswered. Invitations are declined. He spends evenings alone, scrolling through technical articles or watching the same programs without really following them. He no longer enjoys the hobbies he used to use to decompress. Even small pleasures seem distant, as if they belong to someone else.

At work, he becomes increasingly vigilant. He rereads messages several times, worried he has missed something important. He has trouble concentrating during meetings and loses his train of thought when a colleague asks a simple question. He worries that his performance is slipping, and this fear only increases the pressure he puts on himself. He begins staying late to make up for lost focus, then goes home depleted and irritable. He notices that he is quicker to anger than before, especially when startled or interrupted. A dropped mug, a sudden knock at the door, someone coming too close in line at a store—ordinary events now trigger a surge of heat and alarm that seems out of proportion to the moment. He hates the feeling most when it arrives without warning because it reminds him that he cannot will it away.

He carries a deep shame that makes it hard for him to speak about what happened in gendered terms. As a man, he feels he should have been stronger, should have fought harder, should have prevented it. These thoughts circle in his mind relentlessly and leave him feeling defective, as if the assault exposed something permanent and humiliating about him. He sometimes thinks about the event in a detached, almost analytical way, trying to reconstruct every detail and identify where he failed. But the effort does not bring clarity; it only deepens the sense that he is stuck in the same moment, unable to move beyond it.

Now, months later, he still lives with a constant tension between wanting to forget and needing to stay alert. He continues to work, though with more effort, more pauses, and more invisible strain than anyone at the office would guess. He appears composed on the outside, but his days are organized around managing reminders, scanning for danger, and getting through the night. Underneath that discipline is a man who feels changed in a way he does not yet know how to name, carrying fear, anger, and grief in the same body that once felt so dependable.
